sections.heading: Two woods, built to the same standard.
sections.body: We can build a fence for your location from either pine or cedar, and in varying heights. Pine is the budget-conscious choice for a long run of privacy fencing; cedar costs more and holds up better to weather and insects over time. Which one makes sense usually comes down to the length of the run and how long you want to leave it alone.

sections.heading: Privacy, security and shade.
sections.body: Custom pine and cedar privacy fencing built for security, shade, and a clean finished look. Height and picket spacing change what the fence actually does — a full-privacy panel and a spaced picket run are different fences for different problems, and it is worth deciding which one you are buying before the posts go in.

sections.heading: The posts decide how long it lasts.
sections.body: Pickets and rails are the part you see, but they are not the part that fails first. A wood fence usually goes because the posts rotted at the ground line or worked loose in soft soil, and once that starts the rest follows regardless of how good the boards were. Depth, spacing and how the post is set are what buy the years. This is also why a fence that looks fine from the road can still be near the end of its life — push on it, and if the posts move, the fence is telling you something the pickets are hiding. It is worth knowing before you spend money on replacement boards that will outlive what holds them up.

sections.heading: Pick the height for the job, not the look.
sections.body: Height is the decision people most often get wrong, partly because it is hard to picture from a catalogue. Six feet is the usual privacy answer because it breaks sightlines from a neighbouring yard at standing height. Four feet contains pets and marks a front boundary without walling the property off, which is often what a front yard actually wants. Eight feet screens completely where local rules allow it. It is worth knowing that height drives cost more than the extra material suggests, because taller fencing needs deeper posts and more bracing to stay upright in wind. A four-foot fence bought for privacy is money spent on the wrong problem, and it cannot be raised later without starting again.

faqs.q: How tall should a privacy fence be?
faqs.a: Six feet is the usual answer for privacy, because it screens sightlines from a neighbouring yard at standing height. Four feet contains pets and marks a front boundary without closing the property off. Eight feet screens completely where that is permitted locally. Height also changes the price more than most people expect, since it changes post depth as well as material.

faqs.q: Does a wood fence need sealing?
faqs.a: It extends the life, particularly on pine. Cedar tolerates being left alone better than pine does, which is part of what the extra cost buys. Either way the posts fail before the pickets do, so how they were set matters more to the lifespan than what gets put on the surface afterwards.

sections.heading: Sports and court enclosures.

sections.heading: Two numbers change the price.
sections.body: Chain-link is priced by height and by the gauge of the wire, and the right answer depends on what the fence is doing. A dog run and a commercial yard are different fences even though both are chain-link, so it is worth saying which you need before comparing quotes.

sections.heading: Cost per foot is the whole argument.
sections.body: Chain-link covers more ground per dollar than any other fence we build, which is why it keeps winning on long runs, acreage and commercial yards where the job is containment rather than privacy. It also takes weather without needing to be sealed or painted, and a damaged section can be replaced without touching the rest of the run. What it does not do is screen anything, which is the trade you are making. Slats can be woven through the mesh where some privacy is wanted without the cost of a wood run, though they are a compromise rather than a substitute. If the fence exists to keep something in or out over distance, this is usually the right answer.

faqs.q: What height of chain-link do I need?
faqs.a: Four feet contains most dogs and marks a boundary. Six feet is the common choice for security and for keeping larger animals in. Taller runs are used for courts and sports enclosures, where the job is keeping a ball in rather than keeping anything out — those need heavier posts and closer spacing.

sections.heading: Rail count is the real decision.

As containment for larger animals, three rails hold more reliably, because an animal that can get its head through a gap will usually try. Split rail also suits uneven ground better than panel fencing, which is part of why it keeps appearing on acreage where a rigid run would leave gaps at every dip.

sections.heading: Containment and boundary are different jobs.
sections.body: A fence keeping cattle in and a fence marking a property line are built differently. Livestock decides height, spacing and how solid the corners have to be, because the animals lean on it; a boundary run can be lighter. Saying which one you need is the single most useful thing on a first call.

sections.heading: Long runs change the economics.
sections.body: On acreage the cost is in linear feet, so the choice of material matters more than it does on a back garden. Split rail suits pasture and grazing; chain-link covers ground cheaply where containment matters more than looks. We build both, and on a long run it is worth walking the line before deciding.

sections.heading: North Louisiana ground is not flat and not dry.
sections.body: Slope, soft ground and standing water all change how posts have to be set. A fence line that crosses a low spot or a drainage cut needs planning rather than improvising on the day, which is why we would rather look at it than quote it blind.

sections.heading: Animals lean on fences.
sections.body: A boundary fence marks a line; a containment fence resists an animal pushing against it, and the two are built differently even when they look similar from the road. Posts are set deeper and closer, corners and gate posts are braced because that is where the load concentrates, and the rail count is chosen for what is being held rather than for appearance. Two rails suit a boundary or a decorative run. Three hold larger animals more reliably. Pasture also tends to mean longer runs over uneven ground, which changes how the line is laid out — following the contour rather than cutting across it keeps the fence tight and keeps gaps from opening at the low points where an animal will find them.

pages.seoDescription: Commercial fencing in Monroe, West Monroe and Ouachita Parish — business premises, yards, storage and larger properties.

sections.heading: Security first, appearance second.
sections.body: Chain-link is durable, budget-conscious fencing for homes, pets, businesses, and larger properties, and on commercial work it usually wins for the same reason it wins on acreage: it covers the most ground per dollar and it does not hide what is behind it. Where appearance matters at the frontage, ornamental and metal fencing adds security without closing the property off visually.

sections.heading: The gate is the part that gets used.
sections.body: On a commercial site the fence is mostly static and the gate works every day, which means the gate is where wear, cost and frustration concentrate. Width has to suit the largest vehicle that will ever need in, including deliveries rather than just staff vehicles. Hardware takes far more cycles than a residential gate ever will. Where the opening sits relative to the approach matters too: a gate that requires a vehicle to stop on a road to line up will get treated roughly, whichever way it swings. Getting the width and the approach right at the start costs very little; correcting either one afterwards means moving posts.

sections.heading: The yard usually has to keep working.
sections.body: Most commercial fencing goes up around a site that cannot close for the week. Sequencing the work so access stays open is a scheduling question more than a fencing one, and it is easier to solve before we start than halfway through.

sections.heading: Why commercial runs usually end up chain-link.
sections.body: Commercial fencing is normally bought by the foot rather than by the panel, and that changes which material makes sense. Chain-link covers distance more economically than anything else, takes weather without being sealed or painted, and can have a damaged section replaced without disturbing the rest of the run — which matters when the fence surrounds something that has to keep operating. It also makes the yard visible, which is a security advantage as often as it is a drawback. Where appearance matters at a street frontage, the usual answer is to treat that stretch differently rather than to pay for the whole perimeter twice. Height is a separate decision from material and worth settling on its own terms.

sections.heading: A gate is a lever on a post.
sections.body: Every gate is a weight hanging off one side of a post, and the wider the gate the harder it pulls. Most sagging gates are not bad gates — they are gates hung on a post that was set for fence and not for leverage. A gate post wants to be bigger, deeper and better braced than the run it sits in.

sections.heading: Width is the decision that costs money later.
sections.body: A drive gate that is narrow enough to be awkward gets clipped, and a gate that has been clipped never hangs right again. Measure for the vehicle that actually uses it, including the trailer, before settling on a width.

sections.heading: The gate should look like part of the run.
sections.body: We fit gates to wood, chain-link and ornamental fencing so the gate reads as part of the fence rather than as something bolted on afterwards.

sections.heading: Measure for the trailer, not the car.
sections.body: The most common regret on a drive gate is width, and it is the one thing that cannot be adjusted afterwards without moving a post. People measure for the vehicle they drive every day and then discover the gate is tight for a trailer, a mower, a delivery truck or a contractor who needs to get a machine into the back yard. A gate that is slightly too narrow gets clipped, and a gate that has been clipped never hangs true again. Walk it through in your head with the widest thing that will ever need to pass, then add room for the fact that nobody lines up perfectly on a first attempt. Extra width costs very little at the start.

faqs.q: Why do gates sag?
faqs.a: Almost always because the gate post was set for fence rather than for leverage. A gate is a weight hanging off one side of a post, and the wider the gate the harder it pulls. A gate post wants to be bigger, deeper and better braced than the run it sits in — which is cheap to do at the start and expensive to correct afterwards.

sections.heading: The posts usually decide it.
sections.body: Panels and pickets are cheap to replace; posts are not. If the posts are still solid, a repair is nearly always the better buy. When the posts have gone — leaning, rotted at ground level, or pulling out — you are rebuilding the fence around bad foundations, and that is the point at which replacement stops being the expensive option.

sections.heading: Taking it out is part of the job.
sections.body: Removal and haul-off is the part people forget when comparing a replacement to a new build. It is real work — old posts set in concrete do not come out easily — and it belongs in the quote rather than appearing as a surprise.

sections.heading: Worth changing what did not work.
sections.body: A replacement is the one chance to change height, material or layout without paying twice. If the old fence was the wrong height, or the gate was in the wrong place, say so before we start rather than rebuilding the same problem.

sections.heading: How to tell which one you need.
sections.body: The test is the posts. Individual broken pickets, a sagging gate or a couple of damaged panels are repairs, and repairs are worth doing when the structure underneath is sound. Once posts are rotted, leaning or moving when pushed, the arithmetic changes: replacing posts means pulling the fence apart anyway, and a patchwork of new posts under old boards tends to mean returning to the same fence again in a year or two. The other honest signal is how many repairs you have already paid for. A fence that has been fixed three times is usually telling you what it needs. Walking the line and pushing on posts every few feet will answer this faster than any estimate.

sections.heading: Wind finds the weak post.
sections.body: A storm rarely takes a whole fence evenly. It finds the post that was already marginal and takes the sections either side of it, which is why a repair that only replaces the panels tends to fail again in the next blow. We repair leaning posts, damaged panels, broken gates and storm-related fence damage.

sections.heading: A fallen limb is a different job.
sections.body: A tree or a large limb across a fence usually destroys the posts as well as the panels, and sometimes moves the fence line. That is closer to a rebuild of the affected run than a repair, and it is worth knowing which one you are looking at before making a claim.

sections.heading: Send a picture before we drive out.
sections.body: A photograph of the damage from a few feet back tells us more than a description does, and it usually decides whether the job is a repair or a replacement without anyone making a trip.

sections.heading: Photograph it first.
sections.body: North Louisiana weather takes fences down, and the instinct after a storm is to clear the mess. Take photographs before you do. Whether an insurer covers the damage is between you and your policy, but the claim is far easier to make when there is a record of what the fence looked like before anything was tidied, from a few angles, with something in frame for scale. It also helps to note which way things fell, because wind direction and a fallen limb tell a different story from a post that had already rotted. None of that can be reconstructed once the debris is gone. If a fence is down across a boundary or blocking access, secure the gap first and photograph what you moved.

faqs.q: Will my insurance cover a storm-damaged fence?
faqs.a: That is between you and your insurer and depends on your policy, so it is worth asking them before committing to work. What helps either way is photographs of the damage taken before anything is moved or cleared.

Everyday repair is quieter: a gate that sags because the post was set for fence and not for the leverage of the gate, a section a vehicle clipped, a dog that found the one loose board, a chain-link run that is leaning after years of people climbing it. Wood, chain-link, and ornamental fences all come in. Vinyl repairs depend on whether the broken piece is a rail or a post and whether that style is still made. Bring a photo. It often tells us whether to bring boards or to come and look at posts.

sections.heading: Wet soil is why the same repair fails twice.
sections.body: A post reset in the same soft hole, without thinking about water, leans again. Monroe and West Monroe yards after a heavy rain show you where the water sits. A repair on that line either moves the post, sets it so water is not the whole story, or it is a temporary fix and we should say so. Slope changes it too. A fence that stair-steps down toward a drainage ditch needs the low end planned, not improvised. If the line is the property line and you are not sure where that is, sort that out before posts are pulled. Moving a repaired fence is the expensive version of a survey.

sections.heading: Length, material, and whether the posts move.
sections.body: On the call, three things matter: about how many feet are damaged, what the fence is made of, and whether the posts are solid. A phone photo of the worst post and of the whole run from a few steps back is enough for a lot of small repairs. A whole side of a yard wants a visit. We are at 205 Mane St, Ste C, West Monroe. Most repair work is in West Monroe, Monroe, and the rest of Ouachita Parish. If you are comparing a repair to a new fence, the materials calculator and the permit guides are the next stop after this page, especially if the repair is about to become a replacement tall enough that the city cares.

faqs.q: Is a repair worth it?
faqs.a: Usually yes when the posts are solid and the damage is a section, a gate, or some pickets. When the posts are rotted or loose, you are paying to decorate a fence that needs to be rebuilt. We would rather say that on site than sell boards.

faqs.q: Do you repair chain-link and metal fences too?
faqs.a: Yes. Chain-link that is leaning, ornamental fences with a broken picket or a dragging gate, and wood. Vinyl depends on the parts. A photo is the quickest way to know.

faqs.q: How is this different from storm repair?
faqs.a: Storm work is a fence that weather or a tree took down, often with an insurance photo to take first. This page is the ordinary repair: age, a vehicle, a gate, a few bad posts. If a storm did it, use the storm damage page so you photograph it before anything is cleared.

sections.heading: Privacy without a paint can.
sections.body: A vinyl privacy fence does the same job as a wood privacy fence: it breaks the sightline into the next yard. Picket and spaced styles mark a front yard without walling it off. Homeowners in Monroe and West Monroe usually ask about vinyl after they have painted a pine fence once and do not want to do it again. That is a fair reason. Vinyl does not need stain. It also does not hide a bad post. The panels are only as straight as what holds them, and a vinyl fence with a leaning post looks worse than a wood one because the panels stay bright while the line goes crooked.

sections.heading: North Louisiana sun is not a mild test.
sections.body: Summer here is long. Dark vinyl runs hotter and shows heat distortion sooner than a light color, which is why white and clay are the styles you see holding up on streets in West Monroe. We will talk about color on site rather than sell a dark fence that looks sharp in a photo and waves by August. Rails and pickets also expand. A fence built tight on a cold morning can bind a gate in July if the hardware and the gaps were not planned for it. That is a build detail, not a reason to avoid vinyl. It is a reason to build it with the season in mind.

sections.heading: Usually near pine on a short run, not a bargain on a long one.
sections.body: We do not print a dollar-per-foot price. Length, height, gates, and the ground move it too much, and a number given without walking the line gets revised. In relative terms, vinyl privacy often lands near a pine privacy fence and sometimes above it once the gates and the style are counted. Cedar costs more than pine and still wants occasional care. Vinyl is the one you are buying so you can leave the surface alone. Chain-link is cheaper per foot when the job is keeping a dog in a long yard and privacy does not matter. If privacy is the point, vinyl and wood are the conversation, and the permit rules for height are the same either way.

sections.heading: The expensive parts are the ones you do not see.
sections.body: Vinyl posts on a privacy fence need to be set for wind. A six-foot solid panel is a sail in a spring storm coming across open yards in Ouachita Parish. Gate posts need to be heavier than line posts, same as wood, because the gate is a lever. A drive gate that is too narrow gets clipped, and vinyl does not forgive a clip the way a board you can replace does. Measure for the widest thing that will use the drive, including a trailer. We install from our West Monroe shop at 205 Mane St, Ste C, across Monroe and West Monroe. If the fence is new rather than a repair, check the Monroe or West Monroe permit guide before the posts go in. Height and the front-yard rules are local, and they are easier to read first than to rebuild.

faqs.q: Is vinyl cheaper than wood?
faqs.a: Sometimes it is close to pine privacy, and sometimes the style and the gates put it higher. It is not the cheap fence. Chain-link is, when you do not need privacy. Call with the length and the style and we will look at the line before naming a figure.

faqs.q: Does vinyl work in Louisiana heat?
faqs.a: Light colors do better than dark ones. The build has to leave room for the material to move, and the posts have to be set for wind on a solid panel. Those are the details that decide whether it still looks right in a few summers.

faqs.q: Can you match an existing vinyl fence?
faqs.a: Sometimes, if that profile is still sold. A photo of the post, the rail, and the panel from the side tells us whether a repair section will match or whether the run wants to be replaced together.

sections.heading: Security and a boundary, not privacy.
sections.body: An aluminum picket fence lets you see through it. That is the point on a front yard in Monroe, on a commercial frontage where you want the building visible, and anywhere a solid wall would look like the back of the property facing the street. It will not stop a sightline. If that is what you need, the privacy fence page is the wood or vinyl conversation. Ornamental fence marks the line, keeps a casual cut-through honest, and holds a gate. It is a poor choice for a dog that can squeeze pickets, unless the spacing is chosen for that animal and not for the look.

sections.heading: The old iron fences around town explain the choice.
sections.body: There is plenty of older steel and iron fence in Monroe and West Monroe, and a lot of it is being painted because it rusts at the joints. Aluminum ornamental fence is what people switch to so the maintenance is hardware and posts, not a wire brush. It is lighter, which is nice to carry and which means the post has to be set properly or the whole run feels flimsy in a wind. We do not describe it as wrought iron. If you have true iron you want repaired, say that, because repair and a new aluminum run are different work.

sections.heading: The gate is where ornamental fence gets expensive.
sections.body: A walk gate is straightforward if the post is big enough and deep enough. A drive gate is the piece that sags, drags, and gets hit. Width is the decision you cannot undo without moving a post. Measure the vehicle and the trailer, then add room for a bad angle on the way in. On a corner lot, the gate and the fence also have to stay out of the sightline at the intersection. West Monroe and Monroe both treat corner lots differently from a mid-block backyard. The permit guides spell out whose rules apply. Read them before we set a corner post you then have to move.

sections.heading: Front yards, small commercial lots, and pool surrounds.
sections.body: The usual residential job is a front or side yard that a privacy fence would close off, especially on streets where the house is the thing you want to see. Small commercial lots on the West Monroe side use it along the street and chain-link or a taller fence at the back. Pool surrounds are a different rule set: a fence around a pool has to do a safety job, and the city's pool-barrier rules are not the same as a decorative front fence. We will not guess those on a sales page. If the fence is for a pool, say so on the call and check the permit guide for the city you are actually in. We work from 205 Mane St, Ste C, West Monroe, on both sides of the river.

faqs.q: Is aluminum the same as wrought iron?
faqs.a: No. Aluminum ornamental fence is the lower-maintenance stand-in for that look. Existing iron can sometimes be repaired. A new run is usually aluminum, and we will say which one you are buying.

faqs.q: Will it give me privacy?
faqs.a: No. You can see through it. That is why people put it on a front yard. For privacy, look at wood or vinyl.

faqs.q: Can it go around a pool?
faqs.a: Only if it meets the barrier rules for that city, which cover height, gaps, and the gate latch. Tell us it is a pool fence at the start, and check the Monroe or West Monroe permit page before anyone digs.

sections.heading: Six feet is the usual answer, and it is not always allowed.
sections.body: A six-foot solid fence blocks the sightline from a neighboring yard at standing height. Four feet does not, no matter how nice the pickets are. Eight feet screens more and needs a stronger build, and it is the height most likely to run into a local limit. Monroe, West Monroe, and the unincorporated parish do not share one rule. A backyard in the city and a lot outside the city limits can be different jobs. The permit guides on this site point at the city's own text for height, front yards, and corner lots. Read the one that matches the address before you fall in love with a picture of an eight-foot fence.

sections.heading: Same job, different upkeep.
sections.body: Pine is the common privacy fence because it covers the run for less than cedar or a fancy vinyl style. It wants seal if you care how it looks in five years, and the posts still outlast the argument about stain. Cedar costs more and weathers better. Vinyl privacy is the option when you do not want to coat it at all. All three fail the same way if the posts are shallow in wet Ouachita ground: the panels stay pretty and the line leans. A privacy fence is a sail. Spring wind across an open yard in West Monroe will find the weak post. That is why post depth and spacing are the part of the quote worth understanding, not just the price of the board.

sections.heading: The pretty side and the property line are separate questions.
sections.body: People ask which side of the fence the 'good side' faces. That is a build choice and a neighbor choice, and it is cheaper to agree before posts are in the ground. Where the fence sits is not a choice we get to invent. If you are not sure the line is where the old fence was, a survey is less painful than moving a finished run. Shared fences and fences just inside your line get handled differently, and an HOA can be stricter than the city about height, color, and which side faces out. If you have an HOA, their paper rules over a page like this one.

Privacy fences are most of the residential work in Monroe and West Monroe: back yards in neighborhoods off the river, side yards where a patio faces a neighbor, and the occasional full enclose. Chain-link with slats is a compromise when budget is the whole story and full privacy is not. It is not the same fence. If you want a number, we need the approximate length, the height you are allowed to build, and whether a gate has to fit a mower or a truck. The materials calculator will count boards and posts for a length you already know. It will not know your property line or your city's height cap. Those are the permit pages.

faqs.q: How tall should a privacy fence be?
faqs.a: Six feet is the height that actually blocks a standing neighbor. Taller than that depends on the city and, if you have one, the HOA. Four feet will disappoint you if privacy was the reason you called.

faqs.q: Wood or vinyl for privacy?
faqs.a: Wood if you want the lower material cost of pine or the longer-weathering cedar and you will live with some upkeep. Vinyl if you want to stop painting. The posts matter more than that choice. Both need to be set for wet ground and wind.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit?
faqs.a: Often the answer depends on height, the front yard, and whether you are in Monroe, West Monroe, or the parish. Use the permit guide for the place the property actually sits, and call the office if the guide and your lot do not obviously match.

sections.heading: Why this page does not list a price per foot.
sections.body: Twin City Fence does not publish a rate card. A 100-foot pine privacy fence on flat, open ground and a 100-foot fence that steps down a wet slope with two gates and a stump in the line are different jobs, and a single number would be a fiction. Anyone who gives you a firm figure from a phone description, without seeing the line, is guessing. We would rather walk it. What this page can do is put the choices in order so you know what you are comparing when two estimates do not match.

sections.heading: What usually costs more than what.
sections.body: Chain-link usually costs less per foot than the other fences we build. It wins on long runs, dogs, and commercial yards where privacy is not the job. Pine privacy costs more than chain-link and is the usual backyard fence. Vinyl privacy often lands near pine and sometimes above it once style and gates are included. Cedar costs more than pine. Aluminum ornamental is usually the highest per foot of the residential fences we install, because the posts and the gates are a large share of a shorter, more detailed run. Those are relative statements, not a price list. They are also typical of how bids come out in Monroe and West Monroe, not a promise that your yard will sort itself the same way if the ground is difficult.

sections.kicker: The things that move a bid
sections.heading: Length is obvious. The rest surprises people.
sections.body: Height costs more than the extra board suggests, because taller fence needs deeper posts and more brace in the wind. Gates cost more than the same width of fence, and a drive gate costs more than a walk gate. Removing an old fence, especially posts set in concrete, is part of a replacement and it gets forgotten when someone prices 'just the new fence.' Trees, a slope toward a ditch, and soil that stays wet along the Ouachita all add work. So does a corner lot, where the fence may have to sit back so drivers can see. None of that shows up in a national average you found online. If a planning table appears under this page later, it will be labeled as an estimate. Until then, the honest figure is the one from a visit.

sections.kicker: How to get a useful number
sections.heading: Measure roughly, then have us look.
sections.body: Pace the run or step it off. Note the corners and every gate, with the width you actually need. Say what the fence is for: privacy, a dog, cattle, a pool, a shop front. Photos of the line, the worst slope, and any old posts help. Then call or use the form. We are at 205 Mane St, Ste C, West Monroe, and we work in Monroe, West Monroe, and Ouachita Parish. The materials calculator will turn a length into a count of posts and pickets so you can see the scale. It does not price labor or haul-off. The permit guides tell you whether height or the front yard is going to change the design before you pay for the wrong fence. Use both. Then get a number from someone who has stood on the line.

faqs.q: What decides the price of a fence?
faqs.a: Three things, in this order: the type of fence, how long the run is, and what the ground is doing. Slope, trees, soft ground and existing posts all change the work involved, which is why a figure given over the phone without seeing the line tends to move once someone walks it.

faqs.q: Do you repair fences, or only build new ones?
faqs.a: Both. Leaning posts, damaged panels, broken gates and storm damage are all repair work. Whether a repair is worth doing usually comes down to the posts — panels and pickets are cheap to replace, posts are not.

faqs.q: Should I choose wood or chain-link?
faqs.a: Wood if you want privacy or the look; chain-link if the job is containment over a longer run. Chain-link covers more ground per dollar than anything else we build, which is why it tends to win on acreage and commercial yards. They are different fences for different problems rather than better and worse.

faqs.q: Pine or cedar?
faqs.a: Pine is the budget-conscious choice for a long run of privacy fencing. Cedar costs more and holds up better to weather and insects over time. Which one makes sense usually comes down to the length of the run and how long you want to leave it alone.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a fence?
faqs.a: It depends on where the property sits and what you are building, and rules differ between Monroe, West Monroe and the unincorporated parish. Check with your local permitting office before work starts — and if there is an HOA, check with them too, since they often set height and material rules the parish does not.

faqs.q: How close to the property line can I build?
faqs.a: That is set locally rather than by us, and it is worth confirming before posts go in — moving a finished fence is far more expensive than checking first. If you are unsure where the line actually runs, a survey settles it and prevents the argument that a misplaced fence otherwise starts.

faqs.q: Do you build fences for livestock?
faqs.a: Yes. Split rail suits pasture and grazing, and the rail count is the main decision: two rails suit a boundary or a decorative run, three hold larger animals more reliably. Containment fencing is built differently from a boundary run because animals lean on it.

faqs.q: Do you fit gates as well?
faqs.a: Yes, to wood, chain-link and ornamental fencing. The thing worth settling early is width — a drive gate narrow enough to be awkward gets clipped, and a gate that has been clipped never hangs right again. Measure for the vehicle that actually uses it, including the trailer.

faqs.q: What areas do you cover?
faqs.a: We're based in West Monroe. We build fences in Monroe, West Monroe, Calhoun, Sterlington, Swartz, Ruston, Bastrop, and Farmerville. Houses and shops. Call (318) 351-2539 and tell us the address.
